cards.front: Which proteins are best supported as forming or lining the hair-cell transduction pore?
cards.back: TMC1 and TMC2, acting within a complex with partner proteins.
cards.quote: its close relative TMC2 form or line the pore of the transduction channel

cards.front: Conventional hair-cell transduction channels open when the bundle deflects toward its {{c1::tallest row}}.
cards.back: Tip links are thought to pull channels open near their lower ends.
cards.quote: Deflect the bundle toward its tallest row and the tip links are thought to pull channels open near their lower ends.
cards.section: What a transduction current looks like

cards.front: Why does the conventional hair-cell transduction current reverse direction when voltage crosses its reversal potential? Use outward positive.
cards.back: The driving force changes sign: current is inward (negative) below the reversal potential and outward (positive) above it. Use outward positive.
cards.quote: It is inward at negative voltages and would be outward above its reversal potential, near 0 mV.
cards.section: What a transduction current looks like

cards.front: What two structures does a hair-bundle tip link connect?
cards.back: The tip of a shorter stereocilium and the side of its taller neighbour.
cards.quote: Tip links connect the tip of each shorter stereocilium to the side of its taller neighbour.
cards.section: What a transduction current looks like

cards.front: For an ion channel, {{c1::P_open}} is the fraction of time it spends open.
cards.back: Equivalently, it is the probability that the channel is open.
cards.quote: P_open, the open probability: the chance that a given channel is open, or the fraction of time it spends open.
cards.section: One current, three factors

cards.front: For identical hair-cell channels at fixed voltage and ions, what equation gives mean bundle current, and what do its factors mean?
cards.back: I = N × i × P_open: working-channel number × current per open channel × open probability.
cards.quote: the mean current from the bundle is their product, I = N × i × P_open
cards.section: One current, three factors

cards.front: The voltage at which an open channel carries no net current is its {{c1::reversal potential}}.
cards.back: It is denoted E_rev.
cards.quote: E_rev is the reversal potential, the voltage at which no net current flows through the open channel.
cards.section: One current, three factors

cards.front: Why does eliminating a hair-cell current by deleting a gene fail to identify the deleted protein as the pore?
cards.back: I = N × i × P_open. Eliminating any factor silences the current, so a required trafficking or coupling protein could produce the same result.
cards.quote: A knockout is the extreme case: setting any one factor to zero gives zero current
cards.section: One current, three factors

cards.front: A hypothetical hair-cell channel carries -12 pA at -77 mV, with E_rev = +3 mV. Assume a linear current-voltage relation and outward positive. Calculate its unitary conductance.
cards.back: Driving force = -77 - (+3) = -80 mV. g = (-12 pA)/(-80 mV) = 0.150 nS = 150 pS. With outward positive, the negative current is inward.
cards.quote: g = i / (V − E_rev)
cards.section: One current, three factors

cards.front: A hypothetical bundle has 80 identical channels, each carrying -15.0 pA when open, with P_open = 0.25. At fixed voltage and ions, what is the mean current? Use outward positive.
cards.back: I = N × i × P_open = 80 × (-15.0 pA) × 0.25 = -300 pA. With outward positive, this is an inward current of 300 pA.
cards.quote: The mean current you record from a hair bundle is a product, I = N × i × P_open.
cards.section: One current, three factors

cards.front: At fixed voltage and ions, a hypothetical hair-cell bundle loses half its working channels while P_open rises from 0.20 to 0.40. The unitary current stays fixed. What happens to mean current, and why?
cards.back: It stays unchanged: halving N and doubling P_open cancel in I = N × i × P_open. An unchanged mean can therefore hide changes in channel number and gating.
cards.quote: The mean current you record from a hair bundle is a product, I = N × i × P_open.
cards.section: One current, three factors

cards.front: Why must a hair-cell unitary conductance be reported with the recording voltage and ionic conditions?
cards.back: The current-voltage relation is not quite linear, and ions affect permeation. Calcium is thought to impede monovalent cations, changing the measured conductance.
cards.quote: real transduction currents are not quite linear, so a g is quoted with its voltage and ions.
cards.section: One current, three factors

cards.front: How do channel permeation and ion selectivity differ?
cards.back: Permeation describes how ions pass through an open channel; selectivity describes which ions it prefers.
cards.quote: Permeation is how ions pass through the open channel, and selectivity is which ions it prefers.
cards.section: The ladder: what each rung rules out

cards.front: A candidate channel knockout abolishes a hair-cell current. Design a rescue comparison that tests whether the missing gene caused the loss, and state the limit of a successful rescue.
cards.back: Compare mutant cells expressing a working gene with matched mutant cells receiving the control vector, checking expression. Recovery supports the missing gene as the cause. It still cannot distinguish a pore from a required partner: by I = N × i × P_open, restoring any failed factor can restore current.
cards.quote: A protein can be required for a current without forming the pore
cards.section: The ladder: what each rung rules out

cards.front: In neonatal mouse Tmc1/Tmc2 double-null hair cells, conventional current returns after expressing TMC1 alone or TMC2 alone. What functionally important relationship does this establish?
cards.back: Either protein can supply the required function in the neonatal hair-cell environment; rescue does not establish that either acts alone as the pore.
cards.quote: In double-null cultures, expressing either TMC1 or TMC2 restored it.
cards.section: Requirement and rescue

cards.front: A Tmc1-null mouse has early postnatal cochlear transduction currents. Would this justify predicting normal mature cochlear hearing, and why?
cards.back: No. Transient early cochlear Tmc2 expression can mask Tmc1 loss; TMC1 is needed for hearing in the mature mouse cochlea.
cards.quote: Tmc2 is expressed only transiently in the early postnatal cochlea, which is why a Tmc1 single mutant can still show early currents.
cards.section: Requirement and rescue

cards.front: In mouse inner hair cells lacking Tmc2, which replicated permeation change occurs in Beethoven TMC1 channels compared with wild-type TMC1 channels?
cards.back: Reduced calcium permeability.
cards.quote: The Beethoven channels let through less calcium than channels made with wild-type TMC1, and the calcium result has been replicated.
cards.section: Change the protein, not its amount

cards.front: Why does altered selectivity after a TMC1 point mutation strengthen the pore case without proving direct pore lining?
cards.back: It links TMC1 sequence to permeation, but altered complex shape or composition could transmit the effect; partner proteins can also change permeation.
cards.quote: A mutation can act through a change in shape or in the makeup of the complex
cards.section: Change the protein, not its amount

cards.front: A membrane-impermeant cysteine reagent changes permeation after engineered TMC1 has already restored current in Tmc1/Tmc2 double-null mouse hair cells. Which alternative is weakened, and why?
cards.back: Altered synthesis or delivery is weakened: the channels were already working when the reagent was applied. The result instead links an externally accessible residue to permeation in a functioning complex.
cards.quote: Because the current existed before the reagent was added, a change cannot be explained by altered synthesis or delivery of the protein.
cards.section: Change it while it works: acute accessibility

cards.front: Why does chemical accessibility of an engineered TMC1 residue fail to prove that the residue directly lines the pore?
cards.back: An accessible residue beside the pore could also affect permeation when modified. Native partners remain present in this experiment.
cards.quote: Accessibility alone cannot tell a residue that lines the pore from one beside it.
cards.section: Change it while it works: acute accessibility

cards.front: Pressure activates purified, truncated turtle TMC1 and budgerigar TMC2 in liposomes. What does this support, and what limits transfer to mammalian hair cells?
cards.back: It supports intrinsic mechanical responsiveness in a reduced system. Non-mammalian constructs and artificial membranes do not establish native mammalian composition or force coupling; lipid or contaminating-protein currents remain a concern.
cards.quote: This supports intrinsic mechanical responsiveness in a reduced system: the protein alone may conduct and be gated by force.
cards.section: Without the hair cell: purified and transferred proteins

cards.front: Human or mouse TMC proteins produce mechanically activated currents in cultured non-hair cells after assisted surface targeting. Does this establish native tip-link force coupling? Explain.
cards.back: No. It strengthens evidence that TMC proteins can support mechanically gated currents outside hair cells, but assisted targeting in another host does not establish how force from the tip link reaches the native pore.
cards.quote: These are recent, heterologous results with assisted targeting. They strengthen the case for the pore, and they leave the native force coupling open.
cards.section: Without the hair cell: purified and transferred proteins

cards.front: Which mammalian protein family is represented by CALM-1 in the native worm TMC-1 cryo-EM complex?
cards.back: The CIB2 family: CALM-1 is the worm orthologue of mammalian CIB2. The structure does not resolve mammalian CIB2 itself.
cards.quote: CALM-1 is the worm orthologue of mammalian CIB2
cards.section: A pore inside a complex: TMIE, LHFPL5, CIB2 and a worm structure

cards.front: What does loss of detectable stereociliary TMC1 and TMC2 in Cib2-null mouse cochlear cells suggest about N?
cards.back: Working channels at the site are lost or strongly reduced, suggesting lower N. Staining is not a channel count or a test distinguishing assembly, delivery and retention.
cards.quote: although staining is not a channel count, and the result does not say whether CIB2 helps build, deliver or hold the channel there.
cards.section: A pore inside a complex: TMIE, LHFPL5, CIB2 and a worm structure

cards.front: Overexpressed TMC1 and TMC2 reach stereocilia in Tmie-null mouse hair cells, yet no current returns. Which proposed role for TMIE is insufficient to explain this result?
cards.back: A role solely in getting TMC proteins into stereocilia is insufficient. TMIE must support more, such as functional assembly, coupling, gating or permeation. Protein localization alone does not establish working channels or isolate the failed factor.
cards.quote: Overexpressed TMC1 and TMC2 still reached stereocilia, and still gave no current.
cards.section: A pore inside a complex: TMIE, LHFPL5, CIB2 and a worm structure

cards.front: What do reduced unitary current and altered calcium permeability in neonatal Tmie-mutant mouse outer hair cells (permeability tested without functional TMC1) show about TMIE?
cards.back: TMIE shapes permeation properties of the complex. These changes do not establish TMIE as the pore itself.
cards.quote: So TMIE shapes pore properties without being shown to be the pore.
cards.section: A pore inside a complex: TMIE, LHFPL5, CIB2 and a worm structure

cards.front: LHFPL5-null neonatal cochlear cells showed smaller unitary events in one preparation, but later TMC1-only outer hair cells had unchanged unitary conductance. Can LHFPL5 loss universally be said to reduce i? Why?
cards.back: No. The findings differ between preparations. The later authors suggested TMC2-containing channels explained the earlier result and interpreted LHFPL5 mainly as coupling tip-link force; the cause remains unsettled.
cards.quote: Later recordings from Lhfpl5-null outer hair cells whose channels contained only TMC1 found an unchanged unitary conductance
cards.section: A pore inside a complex: TMIE, LHFPL5, CIB2 and a worm structure

cards.front: What change in the hair-cell activation curve defines adaptation during a maintained bundle deflection?
cards.back: The activation curve shifts in the direction of the held deflection.
cards.quote: During a maintained deflection, the activation curve shifts in the direction of the held deflection.
cards.section: Adaptation: the current sags during a held push

cards.front: During a held positive, nonsaturating hair-bundle deflection, inward current magnitude falls while voltage, ions, N and i remain stable. What happens to P_open, and why?
cards.back: P_open falls. With N and i stable, the smaller current magnitude must reflect fewer channels open; adaptation shifts the activation curve in the direction of the held push.
cards.quote: a held positive deflection that does not saturate the current shows it as a declining current
cards.section: Adaptation: the current sags during a held push

cards.front: What do the labels fast and slow adaptation specify in hair cells, and what approximate time scales illustrate them in mouse inner hair cells?
cards.back: They specify kinetics, not molecules: a fast time constant below a millisecond and a slow one of about 11 ms in the cited mouse measurements.
cards.quote: Corns and colleagues (2014) measured a fast time constant below a millisecond and a slow one of about 11 ms.
cards.section: Adaptation: the current sags during a held push

cards.front: Suppose every evidence rung supports a candidate as the hair-cell transduction pore. What further mechanistic question remains, and why does the evidence ladder leave it open?
cards.back: How force from the tip link reaches the pore remains open. The ladder combines requirement, sequence-linked permeation and activity outside hair cells to support pore identity; those rules do not specify the native route of force transmission.
cards.quote: Even a complete ladder says only that the protein forms or lines the pore, not how force from the tip link reaches it.
cards.section: What the ladder settles, and what it does not

cards.front: A new candidate yields mechanically gated current in cultured cells. Design two native hair-cell checks that address necessity and current identity, and state why both matter.
cards.back: Remove the candidate in hair cells with working Tmc1 or Tmc2, matching age and genotype, and ask whether conventional current is lost. Also check tip-link dependence and conventional direction, distinguishing the reverse-polarity PIEZO2-associated current. By the ladder's rule, heterologous activity alone establishes neither native necessity nor identity of the recorded current.
cards.quote: Also check that the current is conventional tip-link transduction, not the reverse-polarity PIEZO2-associated current.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Why should the effect of the Beethoven Tmc1 allele on single-channel current be described as disputed?
cards.back: Laboratories reported smaller currents or reduced conductance in some preparations, but similar conductance in another. This uncertainty does not erase the replicated reduction in calcium permeability.
cards.quote: The unitary-current result is disputed: Beurg and colleagues (2015) found a similar unitary conductance in Beethoven outer hair cells
cards.section: The Beethoven single-channel dispute

cards.front: Two hypothetical hair-cell channels are held at -80 mV. Wild type: i = -16 pA, E_rev = 0 mV. Mutant: i = -12 pA, E_rev = -20 mV. Assume linear relations and matched ions. Compare g; use outward positive.
cards.back: Wild type: g = -16/[-80 - 0] = 0.200 nS. Mutant: g = -12/[-80 - (-20)] = 0.200 nS. Both are 200 pS; smaller inward current reflects smaller driving force. Use outward positive.
cards.quote: At a fixed holding potential, the unitary current then changes because the driving force changed, even if the conductance did not.
cards.section: When selectivity changes, compare conductances, not currents

cards.front: A mutation changes ion selectivity and reduces unitary current at one holding voltage. Design a comparison that distinguishes changed conductance from changed driving force.
cards.back: In matched solutions, measure each genotype's reversal potential and calculate g = i/(V − E_rev), or compare full current-voltage curves. By the driving-force rule, altered selectivity can shift E_rev, changing i even when conductance stays unchanged; raw single-voltage currents cannot separate these explanations.
cards.quote: A mutation that changes which ions pass can also move the reversal potential, depending on the ion gradients in the recording.
cards.section: When selectivity changes, compare conductances, not currents

cards.front: An antibody and an endogenous tag disagree about channel localization in mutant hair cells. Which controls help assess the disagreement, and what inference should remain limited?
cards.back: Use a knockout control to assess antibody signal and verify that the tagged protein retains function. By the localization rung, even a supported localization result establishes presence rather than conduction; staining also cannot count working channels. The reported antibody-versus-tag discrepancy in Cib2 mutants remains unexplained.
cards.quote: Liang and colleagues showed that their tags did not affect TMC1 or TMC2 function
cards.section: Where TMC1 and TMC2 sit in Cib2 mutants

cards.front: A candidate protein produces stretch-activated currents in cultured cells, but native hair cells have not been tested. Why is its identity as the native transduction channel still unestablished?
cards.back: Activity in another host does not establish native necessity or rescue. A mechanically activated current can also differ from conventional tip-link transduction.
cards.quote: gave stretch-activated currents in HEK cells (Murthy and colleagues, 2018) without any test of native hair-cell necessity or rescue.
cards.section: Other mechanically activated currents

cards.front: A neonatal outer-hair-cell conductance gradient persists after Tmc2 deletion. What happens to the hypothesis that TMC2 is required for the gradient, and why?
cards.back: It is contradicted: the gradient exists without TMC2, so TMC2 is not necessary for it. This neonatal result still does not establish the composition of the adult complex.
cards.quote: so TMC2 is not needed to produce a gradient
cards.section: No single hair-cell conductance

cards.front: Why is calcium entry as the driver of fast hair-cell adaptation still an open question?
cards.back: Studies disagree and differ in species, stimulus and bundle-motion handling. In rat outer hair cells, force and displacement steps produce different manifestations of adaptation, complicating comparisons.
cards.quote: The two studies differ in species, stimulus and handling of bundle motion.
cards.section: Adaptation: the calcium question

cards.front: Engineered Myo1c inhibition blocks adaptation in mouse utricular cells, but cochlear slow adaptation can persist without Myo1c activity. How should a model assigning all slow adaptation to Myo1c be revised?
cards.back: Make its requirement preparation-specific rather than universal. By the rule that fast and slow label kinetics, a slow phase does not identify a molecule. Different vestibular and cochlear results challenge a universal motor model while leaving other myosin functions possible.
cards.quote: cochlear slow adaptation did not require Myo1c activity, and the Myo1c result differed between cochlear and vestibular cells.
cards.section: Slow adaptation and Myo1c
